1268.title: Men and women for others
1268.hook: Arrupe's phrase for what Jesuit education should form
1268.howItsDone: Jesuit schools often describe their aim as forming men and women for others, and pair student service with reflection on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pedro Arrupe at Hiroshima, and a house of prayer turned into a hospital. Your line was he turned the house into a hospital.
screen: `HE TURNED THE HOUSE INTO A HOSPITAL.`

segments.voice: A room full of former students of Jesuit schools, gathered in Spain. Doctors, lawyers, business owners: comfortable people, proud of their schooling. At the podium stands the same Pedro Arrupe, now the head of the whole Jesuit order. They might expect a warm speech about the old days. Instead he asks a hard question: have Jesuit schools taught you to care about justice, or only to succeed? Then he offers a short phrase for what those schools are supposed to produce. Tradition says some in the room did not like it. The phrase stayed anyway.
screen: `FORMER STUDENTS, COMFORTABLE, PROUD.` → `HAVE WE TAUGHT YOU JUSTICE?` → `A PHRASE SOME DIDN'T LIKE.`

segments.voice: Men and women for others. In Arrupe's own Spanish the talk was called hombres para los demás, men for others. The aim of Jesuit education, he said, should be to form people who live not for themselves but for God and for others, especially the poor. And he said something harder: that the schools had sometimes failed at it, and that he was asking forgiveness for that. In time, as Jesuit schools welcomed girls and women, the phrase grew into men and women for others, the form you'll hear now. What makes it more than a slogan? Three things. It's about who you become, not only what you do. Volunteering on a Saturday is good; Arrupe was asking about the shape of a whole life. It includes justice, not just charity: he wanted people to ask why someone is hungry, not only to hand them bread. And it's rooted in Jesus himself. In Mark's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says the Son of man "is not come to be ministered unto: but to minister." Served, or serving: the phrase picks a side. Now the honest part. For others can curdle into self-importance, the helper who needs to be needed. The Ignatian answer is the examen: look back each night and ask who the day was really for. For others might be as plain as letting someone go ahead in line, or as big as rethinking what your job is for.
screen: `HOMBRES PARA LOS DEMÁS.` · `WHO YOU BECOME, NOT ONLY WHAT YOU DO.` · `JUSTICE, NOT ONLY CHARITY.` · `WHO WAS THE DAY REALLY FOR?` · then, large: `NOT TO BE MINISTERED UNTO, BUT TO MINISTER.`

segments.voice: Look ahead at the next day for one thing you could do for someone who didn't ask and won't pay you back, and make it concrete: a name, a task, a time. Then ask the second question, the justice one: is there anything behind their need you could learn about, or speak up about? If you pray, offer the plan to God and ask for a clear heart in doing it.
Men and women for others. Pedro Arrupe's phrase for what Jesuit education should form: people who live for God and others, with justice, not only charity. Today's word.
screen: `MEN AND WOMEN FOR OTHERS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: for others. Not to be served, but to serve, with justice as well as charity. Rest well.

1269.title: A Jesuit pope
1269.hook: Francis brought discernment into the language of the whole Church
1269.howItsDone: Following Pope Francis, Catholic parishes, families and Church gatherings speak of discernment as prayerful listening to God and one another before making choices, often alongside the daily examen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, men and women for others: Arrupe's hard question, and a whole life shaped for God and others. Your line was for others.

Discernment can sound like a word for retreat houses and novitiates: quiet rooms, a spiritual director, someone deciding whether to become a priest or a sister. Then a Jesuit from Buenos Aires, Jorge Mario Bergoglio, became Pope Francis, whom you met on day nine hundred thirty-three. The word came with him. It turned up in his letters to the whole Church, in his talks to young people, in what he said to married couples, in the way he asked bishops to meet and listen. A retreat-house word went out into kitchens and parish halls.
screen: `A RETREAT-HOUSE WORD.` → `A JESUIT BECOMES POPE.` → `THE WORD GOES TO THE KITCHENS.`

segments.voice: A Jesuit pope. Francis had made the Spiritual Exercises, had given them to others, and had been a novice master and a Jesuit provincial in Argentina. So when he wrote, the Ignatian vocabulary came along. In his letter on holiness, Rejoice and Be Glad, he gives the closing pages of a chapter to discernment. It isn't only for rare, dramatic decisions, he says, but for daily life: small choices, ordinary days. He recommends something familiar from this path: a sincere daily examination of conscience, looking back over the day with God. And he insists it's a gift to ask for, not a technique to master, and that it means listening: to God, to others, to reality, and especially to the poor. Saint Paul gives the old instruction in the Douay-Rheims: "But prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Prove means test, try out. Francis asked every Catholic to do that, not only people in retreat houses. He also brought the word into how the Church makes decisions, asking for meetings where people would pray, speak freely, listen, and then discern together, rather than simply vote. Why it matters day to day: discernment isn't the same as deciding. Deciding asks what do I want. Discernment asks, in the quiet, which of these good options draws me toward God and others, and which pulls me inward and away? It's the whole Jesuit vocabulary of these weeks, handed to everyone.
screen: `A POPE FORMED BY THE EXERCISES.` · `DISCERNMENT FOR ORDINARY DAYS.` · `A GIFT TO ASK FOR, AND LISTENING.` · `DECIDING VS. DISCERNING.` · then, large: `PROVE ALL THINGS; HOLD FAST THAT WHICH IS GOOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a real, small decision in front of you, and hold the first option for a few breaths, noticing what moves in you: peace, restlessness, energy, dread. Then hold the second the same way, and without deciding yet, notice which draws you outward, toward God and others, and which pulls you inward. If you pray, ask for light.

1270.title: An Ignatian day at home
1270.hook: morning offering, finding God in work, examen at night
1270.howItsDone: Catholics shaped by Ignatian spirituality begin the day with a morning offering, try to notice God through the day's work, and end it with the examen before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Jesuit pope, and a retreat-house word carried into kitchens. Your line was discern.

The alarm goes off. Feet on a cold floor, a kettle, a phone already buzzing, someone who can't find their shoes. No retreat house, no director, no month of silence. Just a weekday. Lately this path has walked through the Spiritual Exercises and the Jesuits who live by them. Today is the last day with them, and it asks a practical question: what does all of that look like in an ordinary house, with dishes in the sink? One Ignatian answer comes in three pieces: morning, middle and night.
screen: `AN ALARM, A KETTLE, LOST SHOES.` → `NO RETREAT HOUSE. JUST A WEEKDAY.` → `MORNING, MIDDLE, NIGHT.`

segments.voice: An Ignatian day at home. Piece one, the morning offering. Before the day runs away, a short prayer hands it to God in advance: the prayers, the work, the joys, the sufferings. One familiar version was spread by a prayer movement founded by a Jesuit, and it comes in more than one wording. It's the Suscipe in miniature: take, Lord, receive, today. Piece two, the middle of the day: God in all things. No extra hour of prayer required. The laundry, the commute, the email, the child's question become places to notice God at work, the way the young Jesuit student learned to find God over his grammar book. Contemplatives in action, at the kitchen sink. Piece three, the examen at night, which you first met on day two hundred thirty-seven. Tradition says Ignatius would let a busy Jesuit shorten other prayers, but not this one. In the Exercises he lays it out simply: give thanks for the day's gifts, ask for light, go back over the hours, ask pardon where you fell short, and look toward tomorrow with hope. It takes a few minutes, and needs no words aloud. The psalm in the Douay-Rheims holds both ends of the day together: "To shew forth thy mercy in the morning, and thy truth in the night." And look who has come along these weeks: the foundation, indifference, the two standards, discernment, the Suscipe, cura personalis, the magis, the Salvadoran Jesuits, Pedro Arrupe, a Jesuit pope. All of it fits into one ordinary day. Tomorrow, a different school of prayer, on a mountain.
screen: `MORNING: HAND THE DAY OVER.` · `MIDDLE: GOD IN ALL THINGS.` · `NIGHT: THE EXAMEN.` · `THE WHOLE JESUIT WAY, IN ONE DAY.` · then, large: `THY MERCY IN THE MORNING, THY TRUTH IN THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last day: find one thing to be grateful for and stay with it, then ask for light to see the day honestly. Walk back through the hours, noticing where you felt close to God or to goodness and where far away, and if something needs forgiving, say so simply. Last, look toward tomorrow; if you pray, do all of it in God's company.
An Ignatian day at home. A morning offering, God in all things through the day, and the examen at night: the Jesuit way, fitted into an ordinary house. Today's word, and the last of the Jesuits.

1271.title: Hermits on Carmel (c. 1200)
1271.howItsDone: Carmelite friars, nuns and lay Carmelites look to Elijah and to Mary as models, and give a central place in their lives to silent, personal prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last day with the Jesuits: a morning offering, God at the sink, the examen at night. Your line was God in all things.

A long green ridge runs down to the sea on the coast of the Holy Land, and at its top a man is crouched on the ground, his face pressed between his knees. He has just come through a very public day: a crowd, an altar, fire from heaven, the story you met on day four hundred ten. Now he has climbed away to pray alone, while his servant keeps going to look out at the sea. The man is the prophet Elijah, Elias in the Douay-Rheims, and the ridge is Mount Carmel.
screen: `A RIDGE ABOVE THE SEA.` → `A PROPHET, FACE TO HIS KNEES.` → `HERMITS ON THE SAME MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Carmelite: someone who belongs to Carmel, to the order that grew up on that mountain. Start with Elijah, because the hermits did. In the third book of Kings, as the Douay-Rheims names it, Elijah stands on Carmel and calls a wavering people to choose the Lord. Fire falls on his offering. Then, the text says, he goes up to the top of Carmel, bows to the ground, and "put his face between his knees." He prays and keeps praying, and his servant keeps going back to watch the sea, until at last a little cloud rises out of the sea, small as a man's foot, and the drought breaks in rain. That's the picture the hermits treasured. Not the fire. The man alone on the mountaintop, praying low and waiting. Much later, tradition says, a small group of Western Christians, pilgrims and penitents from Europe, settled on Carmel as hermits. They lived in caves and small cells on the slope, near a spring that tradition linked to Elijah. They looked to Elijah as their model, and in time dedicated their life to Mary too; tradition says they built a little chapel in her honor. That double inheritance is still in the order's full name: the Brothers of the Most Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel. Later the Carmelites would spread far from the mountain, and saints would come from Spain and France and elsewhere. But it begins small: a few people, a ridge, a spring, and a prophet's posture of waiting prayer.
screen: `ELIJAH ON CARMEL.` · `FACE BETWEEN HIS KNEES, WAITING.` · `HERMITS NEAR A SPRING.` · `ELIJAH AND MARY: A DOUBLE INHERITANCE.` · then, large: `A LITTLE CLOUD, LIKE A MAN'S FOOT.`

segments.voice: Find the quietest small spot within reach, the end of a sofa, a step outside, even a parked car, and sit low, leaning forward a little the way Elijah did. Don't ask for fire; just wait, the way his servant watched the sea. If you pray, pray without words or with one line of a psalm; if not, rest in the quiet of your corner.
Carmelite. One who belongs to Carmel: the order that began with hermits on Elijah's mountain and gave its life to Mary. Today's word.

1272.title: The Rule of Carmel
1272.hook: stay in your cell, meditating day and night on the law of the Lord
1272.howItsDone: Carmelite friars and nuns still take the Rule of Saint Albert as their foundation, and in their houses each has a cell for prayer and rest, with an oratory or chapel at the center of community life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Carmelite: hermits on Mount Carmel, Elijah's mountain, praying low and waiting. Your line was Elijah's mountain.

Good intentions only get a group of hermits so far. The men on Carmel had come to pray, and now there were several of them, sharing a spring and a hillside. They needed to know how to live. So, the text tells us, they asked for a way of life in writing, from Albert, the patriarch of Jerusalem. What came back wasn't a thick book of regulations. It reads like a letter, addressed to the hermits living near the spring on Mount Carmel, and in the middle of it sits one sentence that holds the rest together.
screen: `HERMITS ASK FOR A WAY OF LIFE.` → `A LETTER COMES BACK.` → `ONE SENTENCE IN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: The Rule of Carmel opens with the goal before any rules: to live in allegiance to Jesus Christ and serve him with a pure heart. Each hermit gets a cell of his own. An oratory stands in the middle of the cells, where they gather for Mass. They work with their hands. They keep silence. And then the sentence: each one is to stay in his cell, or near it, meditating day and night on the law of the Lord and keeping watch in prayer, unless some other duty calls him away. Anyone who prays the Psalms hears the echo. Psalm one, in the Douay-Rheims: "on his law he shall meditate day and night." The Rule gives the psalm an address: a small room. Jesus gives it a door, in Matthew: "enter into thy chamber, and having shut the door, pray to thy Father in secret." The cell is not a prison; the Rule says nothing about locking anyone in. The instruction is to stay, which is harder, because staying is a choice made again every hour. And notice the word unless. The Rule expects interruptions: work, a brother who needs help, the business of the house. The hermit goes, does what's needed, and comes back. The cell is home base, not a hiding place. The Rule promises no quick results. It asks the hermit to come back, again and again, to the same small room, and keep watch there in prayer.
screen: `FIRST THE GOAL: ALLEGIANCE TO CHRIST.` · `A CELL, AN ORATORY, WORK, SILENCE.` · `STAY IN YOUR CELL, OR NEAR IT.` · `UNLESS A DUTY CALLS: GO, THEN RETURN.` · then, large: `ON HIS LAW HE SHALL MEDITATE DAY AND NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Let the room you're in be your cell for a little while, and don't get up for anything. If you pray, pray the psalm's line slowly or sit before God without words; if you don't, rest your attention on the room itself, its sounds, its light, the chair under you. When the urge comes to check something or fetch something, notice it, and stay.

1273.title: The brown scapular
1273.hook: a small cloth worn as a sign of belonging to Mary, from Carmelite tradition
1273.howItsDone: Catholics who wish to wear the brown scapular are enrolled, usually by a priest, in a short rite of blessing; afterward they wear it under their clothes, and a worn-out scapular can be replaced.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rule of Carmel and its center: stay in your cell, meditating day and night on the law of the Lord. Your line was stay in your cell.

At the beach, or in a locker room, it sometimes shows up: two little squares of brown wool on a pair of strings, one resting on the chest, one on the back. It isn't jewelry. It isn't a charm. People who wear it often tuck it under a shirt where nobody sees it. Ask what it is and you may get a short answer: it's my scapular. You met it briefly on day one thousand eight. Today is the longer answer, and it starts with a piece of clothing much bigger than two squares of wool.
screen: `TWO SQUARES OF BROWN WOOL.` → `NOT JEWELRY, NOT A CHARM.` → `IT STARTS WITH CLOTHING.`

segments.voice: A scapular, in the first place, is part of a religious habit: a long strip of cloth worn over the shoulders, hanging down front and back, like an apron for both sides. The Carmelite habit has one, in brown. Over time, people who weren't friars or nuns wanted a share in Carmel's life of prayer. The small brown scapular is that share: the big garment shrunk to two little panels, so a baker or a nurse can wear it under ordinary clothes. Carmelite tradition says Our Lady gave the scapular to an English Carmelite, Simon Stock, as a sign of her protection. Some historians question the details of that story, and the devotion doesn't ask anyone to settle them first. What the Church does say is plainer. The scapular is a sacramental: a sign, blessed by the Church, that points beyond itself. It doesn't work by itself, like a lucky coin. It means something only when it's joined to a life: prayer, the sacraments, trying to live as Mary lived. Wearing it says, I belong to Mary's family, and through her, to her Son. John's Gospel has the scene this belonging grows from. At the cross, Jesus gives his mother to the disciple he loved, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold thy mother. And from that hour, the disciple took her to his own." Clothing often says who you belong to: a team jersey, a uniform, a wedding ring. The scapular is the same instinct, worn quietly, close to the heart.

1274.title: The Way of Perfection
1274.hook: Teresa's three foundations: love, detachment, humility
1274.howItsDone: Carmelite nuns, and others who learn prayer from Teresa, read The Way of Perfection as a guide to community life and to prayer, including its slow commentary on the Our Father.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the brown scapular: the Carmelite habit in miniature, worn as a sign of belonging. Your line was a sign of belonging.

A handful of nuns in a small, poor convent in Ávila have a request for the woman who founded it: teach us to pray. She is Teresa, the Spanish Carmelite you first met on day twenty, who had pushed to start a house where the sisters could live the old Rule more strictly. She agrees, and she writes them a book. But when they open it, expecting to go straight to the prayers, she makes them wait. Before a single word on how to pray, she talks about how to live.
screen: `TEACH US TO PRAY.` → `TERESA WRITES A BOOK.` → `BUT FIRST, HOW TO LIVE.`

segments.voice: Teresa calls the book The Way of Perfection, and she lays down three foundations. First, love for one another. Not a warm feeling about the community in general, but the daily kind: patience with the sister who annoys you, real concern when someone is sick. She warns against two failures: too little love, and a clingy love that plays favorites. It echoes John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "That you love one another, as I have loved you." Second, detachment from created things. Not hating the world; not being owned by it, by comfort, by possessions, even by your own reputation. Third, humility. And here she does something unexpected. She lists humility last, but calls it the most important of the three, because it holds the others together. Why build prayer on these? Because, for Teresa, prayer isn't a technique you can run while the rest of life goes on unchanged. A person who resents everyone at breakfast will bring that resentment into the chapel. So she starts lower, in the kitchen and the hallway. Only then does the book turn to prayer, and when it does, it walks slowly through the Our Father, the prayer the sisters already knew by heart. Her order of things works outside a convent too. For Teresa, an hour of prayer is shaped by the hours around it: how you spoke to people, what you clung to, whether you needed to win.
